extracted.intended_audience: researchers and scholars studying peer review, scientometrics, and science policy (journal editors, modelling researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the quality and efficiency of journal peer review using an agent-based simulation of authors and referees under different reciprocity and fairness strategies. The rubric focuses on measurable metrics (evaluation bias, resource loss, reviewing expenses, inequality) and behavioural scenario definitions used to assess peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of peer review (screening function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality: the ability of peer review to ensure that only the best submissions are eventually published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a restrictive definition used in the paper (excludes constructive feedback and journal reputation functions). It is operationalised by comparing published items under the simulation to an optimal situation where submissions are published according to their real value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency: the ability of peer review to achieve quality by minimizing the resources lost by authors and the expenses incurred by referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured jointly with quality: minimize resource loss for unpublished authors and reviewing expenses for referees while maintaining screening performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation bias (percentage of errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation bias: measured as the percentage of errors made by referees by calculating the discrepancy between the optimal publication outcome (submissions published according to their real value) and the actual situation in each simulation step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the primary quantitative indicator of peer review quality in tables. The paper notes an evaluation bias default parameter b = 0.1 for reliable referees and reports scenario results (e.g., values in Table 2 and 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource loss (authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resource loss: the amount of resources wasted by (unpublished) authors compared with the optimal solution (where only the best authors were published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculated per simulation condition and presented as percentage. Used to evaluate efficiency (authors' wasted investment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing expenses (referees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing expenses: the resources spent by agents for reviewing compared with the resources invested by submitting authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computed from a reviewing cost formula (S) depending on referee resources R_r, real quality of the author's submission Q_alpha and referee's expected quality mu_r. The paper assumes expenses grow linearly with submission quality and are proportionally dependent on agent resources; results reported as percentages in tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee reliability (reliable behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable referees: ability to provide a consistent and unequivocal opinion which truly reflected the quality of the submission; they do the best they can and spend all needed resources for reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modelled with a normal distribution of expected quality and a narrow standard deviation of evaluation score from real value (σ = R(α)/100). There remains a chance for some evaluation bias (b = 0.1), which increases with the difference between referees' expected quality and author submission quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee unreliability (type I and II errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable referees: commit type I and II errors (recommending low-quality submissions or rejecting publishable ones), spend fewer resources, and systematically under- or over-estimate submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modelled with reduced reviewing expense s = 0.5 and parameters for underrating u = 0.1 (evaluation ≈ -90% of real quality) and overrating o = 1.9 (+90% of real quality). Empirical studies cited suggest such errors are frequent in grant reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness criterion for reciprocal judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness: authors measure the fairness of a referee's opinion by comparing the real quality of their submission and the evaluation rate received; if the referee evaluation approximated the real value (i.e., ≥ -10%), the referee is judged reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 'fairness' scenario, agents reciprocate positively when their assessment of past referees meets this pertinence threshold, making reciprocity norm-based rather than self-interested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect reciprocity (author-referee reciprocity based on publication outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect reciprocity: agents are influenced by their past experiences as authors when selected as referees, reciprocating positively if their past submission was accepted and negatively if rejected, irrespective of pertinence of the referee evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This models self-interested reciprocity where past publication success, not fairness or pertinence, drives future reviewing reliability; can increase evaluation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reciprocity (baseline scenario)
rubrics_metrics.description: No reciprocity scenario: agents have a random probability of behaving unreliably when selected as referees; this probability is constant over time and unaffected by past experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the benchmark for comparing reciprocity and fairness scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author reciprocal behaviour: self-interested vs fair authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Author behaviour variants: 'self-interested authors' react to publication outcome (invest i=1 if published, i=0.1 if rejected) regardless of evaluation pertinence; 'fair authors' invest or disinvest based on whether they received a pertinent evaluation, not merely publication outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author investment i affects subsequent submission quality and system dynamics; 'fair authors' support robustness of peer review quality even under competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication rate / selectivity (p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication rate p: the proportion of submissions accepted (tested values in simulations: 0.25, 0.50, 0.75), representing competition or selectivity in the publication environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher selectivity changes trade-offs between quality and reviewing costs; scenario outcomes vary by p (results reported in Tables 2–4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gini index for inequality of resource distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Gini index: measures inequality of resource distribution among agents (0 = complete equality, 1 = single agent controls all resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess systemic consequences of peer review regimes; results show better quality/efficiency scenarios often correspond to higher inequality (e.g., 'fair authors' produce high Gini in competitive environments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalisation of submission quality from resources (μ and σ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission quality μ derived from agent resources R via a velocity parameter v (μ increases with R); actual submission quality follows normal distribution N(μ, σ) with σ varying proportionally to resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model parameter v (e.g., v=0.1) determines how many resources are needed to reach given quality levels; allows stochasticity where top scientists can produce low-quality submissions and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing cost formula and assumptions (S)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing cost S depends on referee resources R_r, real quality of author's submission Q_α and referee's expected quality μ_r; reviewing is resource-intensive and agent resources determine reviewing quality and cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes reviewing expenses grow linearly with author submission quality and are proportionally dependent on agent resources; if matched with similar-quality submissions referees allocate 50% of resources to reviewing (model rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Winner-takes-all assumption (cost of rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Winner-takes-all rule: if not published, authors lose all resources invested prior to submitting (no resubmission market in the model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simplification that amplifies stakes and affects resource dynamics; authors' investments and subsequent resource multipliers depend on publication success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measures for ex-ante validity of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested ex-ante measures: length of referee report text (longer assumed higher quality), editor-assigned ratings of referees as proxy for review quality, or number of reports a referee was involved in (assumed higher involvement implies higher quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed as feasible empirical proxies to test model findings; can be applied across representative journals to measure referee reliability prior to publication outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measures for ex-post validity of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested ex-post measures: subsequent citations of published articles and the fate of rejected submissions (e.g., later acceptance elsewhere) as indicators of peer review validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combined ex-ante and ex-post measures can build statistical measures of referee reliability and allow testing of reciprocity/fairness effects empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of matching and editorial role
rubrics_metrics.description: Random 1-to-1 matching of authors and referees and exclusion of editors from reciprocity dynamics are modelling assumptions that shape outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes these as simplifications (editors could provide reputation-building room) and suggests that relaxing them is important for future research; users applying the rubric should account for these assumptions when comparing to real systems.
